summary: Turning to the great crowds traveling with Him, Jesus tells them that following Him costs everything and urges them to count the cost before they begin.
key_insight: The builder and the king each sit down to ask whether they have enough. Jesus’ conclusion is not that they should make sure they do, but that a disciple must “forsake all that he has” (v. 33). Counting the cost of following Jesus means discovering that it costs everything.
story: Great crowds were traveling with Jesus. He turned and said to them, “If anyone comes to Me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he cannot be My disciple. And whoever does not bear his cross and come after Me cannot be My disciple.”

Then He asked them to think like a builder. Who starts a tower without first sitting down to count the cost, to see whether he has enough to finish it? If he lays the foundation and cannot finish, everyone who sees it will mock him: “This man began to build and was not able to finish.”

Or what king goes to war without first sitting down to consider whether his ten thousand can meet an enemy coming against him with twenty thousand? If not, while the other army is still a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for conditions of peace.
“So likewise, whoever of you does not forsake all that he has cannot be My disciple.”

“Salt is good; but if the salt has lost its flavor, how shall it be seasoned?” Such salt is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile; people throw it out. “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!”

scene.label: “Hate”
scene.text: In Hebrew idiom, to “hate” could mean to love less or to put second. Genesis says Jacob loved Rachel “more than Leah” and calls Leah “unloved” (Genesis 29:30–31). Matthew records Jesus’ meaning in plain terms: “He who loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me” (Matthew 10:37).

scene.label: An unfinished tower
scene.text: A tower might be a watchtower in a vineyard (Isaiah 5:2) or a farm building for storing crops. A foundation with nothing on it stood in plain view for years, a standing joke at the owner’s expense.

scene.label: Conditions of peace
scene.text: A king outnumbered two to one had little choice but to send envoys while the enemy was still far off and accept his terms. Some see a further point here: Jesus’ hearers themselves face a greater King, and wisdom is to make peace with Him on His terms.

scene.label: Salt for the soil
scene.text: Luke alone mentions the land and the dunghill. Small amounts of salt were used on soil and in manure as fertilizer. Salt that had lost its strength could not even do that.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records this address to the crowds, given on the road to Jerusalem where Jesus Himself will bear the cross. It follows straight from the great supper, where invited guests were too busy with a field, oxen and a wife to come; here Jesus says that family, possessions and life itself must yield to Him. Matthew has some of the same sayings in other settings (Matthew 10:37–38; 5:13), but only Luke has the tower and the king.

seeing.reveals: Jesus does not hide the cost to keep a crowd; He turns and tells them. He claims a loyalty above father, mother, spouse and one’s own life, a claim only God can rightly make.
seeing.living: Do not follow Jesus on a wave of enthusiasm with the crowd. Sit down and count, and you will find that the cost is everything you have. Then give it to the One who walked the road to the cross ahead of you.
seeing.ponder: What do you still hold back as yours, not His?

preaching.big_idea: Following Jesus costs everything; count the cost, then give Him all you have.
outline: The builder: count before you begin (28–30)
The king: surrender while there is time (31–32)
preaching.watch_for: Three times Jesus says “cannot be My disciple” (vv. 26, 27, 33). The two parables stand between the second and the third, and the third tells what the counting reveals.
